name: Horny goat weed (Epimedium)

card.summary: A Chinese medicinal herb sold as a libido and erection supplement; its flavonoid icariin inhibits PDE5 in the lab, but human trial evidence is minimal.
card.aka: Epimedium, yin yang huo, barrenwort, icariin
card.note: Evidence for sexual benefit comes mainly from animal and in vitro work; no published human trial on libido was found.

quick.overview:
Horny goat weed refers to plants of the genus Epimedium, used for centuries in traditional Chinese medicine as a kidney and yang tonic. The supplement form is typically E. grandiflorum or extracts standardized to icariin, sold for libido and erectile function.

Icariin is a weak PDE5 inhibitor in vitro, and animal studies report improved erectile function. Wikipedia states there is little clinical evidence to date, and a recent review says clinical efficacy still needs confirmation in randomized trials.
quick.mechanism: In animal and cell studies icariin has been reported to act through nitric oxide/cGMP signaling, Rho kinase inhibition and weak PDE5 inhibition, the same enzyme targeted by sildenafil and tadalafil, though at far lower potency.
quick.risks: Human safety data are limited. It is sold as a dietary supplement; a US homeopathic-labelled testosterone-support product listing it advises consulting a physician if pregnant or breastfeeding. Interaction data with PDE5 inhibitor drugs are not established in the sources reviewed.

lead: Horny goat weed is the common English name for plants of the genus Epimedium (family Berberidaceae), most of which are native to China [1][2]. The Chinese name yin yang huo is rendered literally as lascivious goat herb [1]. Traditional Chinese medicine has used it as a tonic for kidney yang deficiency, including low libido and fatigue [2][3].

Its supposed aphrodisiac activity is attributed to icariin, a prenylated flavonoid that has been described as a weak PDE5 inhibitor in vitro [1]. Wikipedia states clinical effects are unknown and there is little clinical evidence to date [1]. Reviews of icariin describe erectogenic effects in animal models and say clinical confirmation in high-quality trials is still needed [4][5].

paras: Traditional Chinese medicine uses the aerial parts for kidney-tonifying and yang-strengthening purposes, and the genus is documented for sexual dysfunction and a range of other traditional indications [3]. Western supplements sell Epimedium or icariin extracts for libido, erectile function and vitality [2]. A 2014 paper reviewed sexual-enhancement products sold online containing yohimbine, maca, horny goat weed and Ginkgo biloba [6].
No dedicated randomized trial of horny goat weed or icariin for libido or erectile function was found among the sources reviewed. Wikipedia states there is little clinical evidence to date [1].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists small human studies of icariin for other purposes, including a pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers, and studies in bipolar disorder with substance use and Gulf War illness [7]. A 2010 study in vitro and in animals reported erectogenic and neurotrophic effects of icariin [8]. A 2026 review of icariin in erectile dysfunction summarized mechanisms in animal models (nitric oxide/cGMP activation, Rho kinase and PDE5 inhibition) and concluded clinical efficacy needs confirmation in high-quality randomized trials [4].

Icariin is a flavonoid glycoside; the genus contains more than 260 compounds, mostly prenylflavonoids [3]. Reviews describe actions on the nitric oxide pathway, neuroprotection, bone and anti-inflammatory and anticancer effects in laboratory models [5][9]. The relative PDE5 potency of icariin is much lower than that of approved drugs [1].
Systematic human safety data are limited. A US product label combining horny goat weed with other herbs advises consulting a health professional if pregnant or breastfeeding [10].

The English name derives from a story in which a goat herder noticed increased sexual activity in his flock after they ate the plant; the name barrenwort comes from a historical belief that it could cause infertility in women [2]. It appears in multi-herb men's testosterone and libido products [10].
